name: Gelatin / bone broth

image.caption: Amino Acid Composition in Gelatin chart

lead: Gelatin and bone broth are collagen-derived foods. Gelatin is made by partially breaking down animal collagen, mostly from pork skin, bones and cattle hides, and bone broth is a long-simmered stock in which collagen converts to gelatin. Wellness and looksmaxxing communities eat them to support skin, hair and joints.

Proponents reason that eating collagen-derived amino acids supplies building blocks for skin and hair. Regulators and reference sources report that a cause-and-effect link between ingested collagen hydrolysate and joint maintenance has not been established, and no studies of appearance outcomes were found.

paras: People drink bone broth as a daily or regular warm drink or cooking base, or eat gelatin as dessert or stirred into drinks. It is used as part of an overall diet alongside other protein. Users who report skin or hair changes describe weeks to months.

Gelatin is a protein food and is generally treated as low risk, though some people are allergic to gelatin in injected drugs. It is not suitable for vegetarian, halal or kosher practice depending on the source.

chain: Building blocks for skin and hair
angle.text: Fans eat gelatin and bone broth because collagen-derived amino acids are thought to supply building blocks for skin and hair. Reference sources report that a link between ingested collagen and joint maintenance has not been established, and no appearance studies were found.

lead: Gelatin and bone broth are collagen-derived foods. Gelatin is made by partially breaking down animal collagen, mostly from pork skin, pork and cattle bones and cattle hides, and gels when cooled; bone broth is a long-simmered stock of bones and connective tissue in which collagen converts to gelatin and thickens the liquid. [1][2]

In looksmaxxing and wellness circles they are eaten as inexpensive sources of the amino acids found in collagen, with the aim of supporting skin firmness and hydration, hair, nails and joint comfort that lets people keep training. [3][4] Collagen is the main structural protein of skin, tendon and bone, and glycine, proline and hydroxyproline make up roughly half of gelatin's amino acids, which is the basis of the reasoning that eating them supports connective tissue. [2][5]

Research has examined collagen products rather than broth itself. A 2023 meta-analysis of 26 randomised trials of hydrolysed collagen supplements reported better skin hydration and elasticity than placebo over 2 to 12 weeks, while a reference article on collagen states there is no good evidence that ingested collagen affects skin health. [6][5] A 2011 EFSA opinion found no established cause-and-effect link between collagen hydrolysate and joint maintenance, and a systematic review of collagen peptides with exercise reported benefits mainly for joint function and pain. [2][7]

paras: Gelatin is a translucent, flavourless ingredient that absorbs five to ten times its weight in water and sets when cooled. Commercial gelatin is a by-product of the meat and leather industries, made through pretreatment, acid, alkali or enzymatic hydrolysis, hot-water extraction, refining and drying. [2] Wikipedia lists uses in jelly, gummy sweets and marshmallows, in capsule shells and as a vaccine stabiliser, and in cosmetics, where hydrolysed collagen is used in creams as a conditioner and moisturiser. [2] Dry gelatin is nearly all protein but lacks tryptophan and is low in several other amino acids; glycine, proline and hydroxyproline make up about half of its amino acids. [2][8]

Stock is a savoury cooking liquid made by simmering bones, meat, seafood or vegetables, and connective tissue releases gelatin that thickens it. Roasted-bone brown stock and raw-bone white stock are classic kitchen forms. [1] Some cooks use broth and stock interchangeably; others separate them by bone content, cooking time or seasoning. [1] Home cooks and brands sell long-simmered broths, pressure cookers shorten preparation, and powders, gelatin and collagen products are positioned as convenient equivalents. [1]

Collagen is the body's most abundant structural protein; types I and III account for over 90 percent of human collagen, and type I is found in skin, tendon and bone. [5] Its triple helix has glycine at nearly every third position, proline makes up about 17 percent, and hydroxyproline stabilises the helix. [5] Vitamin C is a cofactor for the enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine, which is why long-term deficiency impairs collagen synthesis and causes scurvy. [5] Skin ageing brings dermal thinning, collagen loss and alteration, and reduced hydration, and chronic UV exposure further disorganises collagen and elastic fibres. [5]

Proponents reason that eating collagen-derived amino acids supplies materials for the skin's matrix. Wikipedia's collagen article notes that ingested collagen is digested into peptides and amino acids and says the elasticity of skin depends more on elastin than collagen. [5] Pairing gelatin with vitamin C is a common community habit and rests on collagen's biochemistry. [9][5]

Wikipedia's gelatin article dates early uses to 1337, when it appears as paper sizing in Europe, and a jellied meat-broth recipe to Le Viandier around 1375. [2] An English production patent followed in 1754, d'Arcet developed acid and steam extraction from bones in 1812, Peter Cooper patented a gelatin dessert powder in the mid-nineteenth century, and Knox Gelatin was founded in New York in the late nineteenth century. [2] The article also notes a 10th-century Arabic cookbook with a gelatin-like dish. [2]

subs.h: Bone broth as a health food
paras: Wikipedia dates the bone-broth health trend to the early 2010s and credits the 2014 book Nourishing Broth with boosting it; the same article says there is no scientific evidence to support many of the claims made for broth. [1] The Weston A. Price Foundation, co-founded by Sally Fallon Morell and Mary G. Enig in 1999, promotes minimally processed traditional foods including bone stocks, and has been criticised by Quackwatch and Science-Based Medicine, according to Wikipedia. [10] Grogu sipping broth in a 2019 episode of The Mandalorian became an internet meme. [1]

A looksmax.org thread titled as a guide to collagen supplements calls gelatin the best and cheapest option and points to a systematic review of oral collagen in 11 studies and 805 participants, covering skin ageing, xerosis and cellulite, as supporting skin benefits; a poster in the thread reported noticing changes. [3] On T Nation, members mention beef gelatin used to thicken protein-rich meals and bone broth as a food during illness or low-carb eating, without appearance claims. [11][12][13]

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 26 randomised trials with 1,721 participants who took hydrolysed collagen for 2 to 12 weeks. [6] Skin hydration improved versus placebo (standardised mean difference 0.63) and so did elasticity (0.72); effects were somewhat larger with use over eight weeks, and fish-derived collagen was described as most effective for hydration. [6] The authors listed limitations including varied doses and forms, small trials and risk-of-bias concerns, and called for larger trials. [6] The reference article on collagen, by contrast, states there is no good evidence that ingested collagen affects collagen production or skin health. [5]

A randomised study of vitamin C-enriched gelatin before intermittent activity measured collagen synthesis, a marker of connective-tissue turnover. [9] A systematic review of 15 randomised trials of collagen peptides with exercise found the most benefit for joint function and pain, with some improvements in body composition, strength and recovery. [7] A trial in active adults examined collagen peptides for function, pain and physical and mental outcomes. [14] EFSA concluded in 2011 that a cause-and-effect relationship between collagen hydrolysate and joint maintenance had not been established. [2]

A 2025 review of bone broth's nutrients examined amino acids and minerals in relation to gut barrier function and inflammation, drawing on animal and human studies. [4] A 2013 paper in Medical Hypotheses reported that organic chicken broths made with bones, with meat only, and with skin and cartilage contained measurable lead; a NutritionFacts video describing it said all three exceeded a per-cup limit and that skin-and-cartilage broth was highest. [15] The same video's page mentions a later study reporting low lead and cadmium in bone broth. [15]

Gelatin is a protein food, but allergic reactions to gelatin in injected drugs and vaccines are documented and have led to its voluntary removal from some vaccines, for example in Japan. [2][16] Alpha-gal syndrome, a delayed allergy to mammalian meat, is a separate condition managed by avoiding mammalian products. [17] Regulators in the EU judged the disease-transmission risk from bovine bone gelatin very low, and the US FDA's 2016 rule treats gelatin made by standard processes as not a prohibited cattle material. [2] Gelatin sources matter for vegetarian, halal and kosher practice; fish gelatin is an alternative. [2][18]

No studies of dietary gelatin or bone broth for appearance outcomes were found. Related human research on collagen supplements is described above: a 2023 meta-analysis for skin hydration and elasticity, a 2021 systematic review and a 2017 randomised trial on collagen peptides or gelatin with exercise, and a trial in active adults. [6][7][9][14] These concern collagen peptides or gelatin supplements, not broth.

lore.intro: Looksmax.org members promote gelatin as an inexpensive collagen source for skin; T Nation members mention gelatin and bone broth mainly as cooking ingredients and training-diet foods. [3][11][12]
